prompt: What NASA datasets are available for NO2 column density over New Jersey?
answer_text:
Exploratory
For NO2 tropospheric vertical column over New Jersey, three NASA/NASA-affiliated satellite datasets are catalogued: TEMPO (hourly, North America only), OMI/Aura (daily, global), and TROPOMI/Sentinel-5P monthly mean (global). All report the quantity "no2_tropospheric_column" in molecules/cm^2. TEMPO is the best fit for current, high-cadence NJ coverage (checked availability: data present for 2026-11-10, 5 granules). OMI_NO2's catalogue record ends 2026-03-15, so a recent date (2026-11-10) falls outside its record and returned no data. TROPOMI monthly-mean has ~58-day latency, so the 2026-10 month is not yet published. These calls only established presence/metadata, not actual pixel values; the polygon handle for New Jersey (polygons_35cfebcfaf8010e6b3180353e2b24951) was used as the area in the availability checks.

prompt: Compare TEMPO NO2 over New Jersey between June 2025 and June 2026 — did it change?
answer_text:
Exploratory
I pulled TEMPO tropospheric NO2 column data over New Jersey for June 2025 and June 2026 and compared the two periods. Important caveat on data coverage: for both months, only 1 of the 30 requested days had valid (cloud/quality-passed) data after masking — 29 days in each period were gaps, not filled — and the valid area was reduced to just 3 grid cells (the "only_candidate" TEMPO_NO2 L3 product). So this comparison rests on a single day's snapshot per period, not a robust monthly climatology.

With that caveat, the area-weighted mean tropospheric NO2 column was about 2.66 mol/m² in June 2025 vs about 5.32 mol/m² in June 2026 — a +100% increase (mean absolute difference +2.66 mol/m², paired at the one location/day pair available, 100% of the 3 cells paired). The single highest-value cell in both periods sits at lat 40.0, lon -75.0 (near the Philadelphia/Trenton corridor). The spread (sample std dev across cells) was large relative to the mean in both periods (±1.53 for 2025, ±3.06 for 2026), reflecting the very small, non-random sample.

Given only one valid day per month survived masking (due to cloud cover or missing granules on the other 29 days), this doubling should be read as an observation from two isolated days, not a validated trend in NO2 levels over New Jersey between the two Junes. It does not tell us whether the surface-level air quality (ppb) changed, since satellite column density (mol/m² or molecules/cm²) is a different physical quantity than a ground monitor's surface concentration.

prompt: Compare the ground NO2 monitors with TROPOMI satellite NO2 over Newark NJ for January 2024.
answer_text:
Exploratory
I could not complete a direct comparison because the ground side has no usable data. The only EPA AQS NO2 monitor findable near Newark, NJ is site 34-017-0006, which AQS lists as measuring NO2 during January 2024, but it lies about 83 km outside the Newark area boundary (Newark's AQS network apparently has no in-area NO2 monitor), and every attempt to pull its actual values — daily readings (Jan 2024, and even expanded to Oct 2023–Jan 2024), daily summaries, quarterly summaries, and the annual summary — returned "insufficient_evidence": AQS has no submitted NO2 measurements for that monitor over these periods, despite it being registered for the parameter. So there is no ground NO2 time series to compare.

On the satellite side, TROPOMI_NO2 tropospheric-column data was retrieved successfully for Newark for 1–31 Jan 2024 (31 daily granules, 100% valid cells, no missing days). The area mean tropospheric NO2 column ranged from about 1.0 to 4.0 mol/m² over the month (regional_series), with a monthly mean of about 2.5 mol/m² (aggregate_time), fairly uniform across the ~10x10 grid (min=max=2.5 in the aggregated map, i.e. little spatial variation at this resolution). A map of the January mean column with the (out-of-area) monitor location overlaid was rendered.

Bottom line: a ground-vs-satellite comparison for Newark NO2 in January 2024 cannot be made — satellite tropospheric-column NO2 is available and summarized, but no EPA AQS surface NO2 monitor inside or near Newark reported usable data for this period, so there is no ground value to set against the satellite column. Note also that even if ground data existed, a satellite tropospheric column (mol/m²) and a surface-level concentration (ppb) are physically different quantities and would need to be framed as two distinct measurements of the same event, not equated.

prompt: Show me what ozone looked like across the OTC on 2024-07-15.

checks.reason: the ground source was used (monitors/byBox queried)

answer_text:
Exploratory
I retrieved NASA TEMPO total-column ozone (TEMPO_O3TOT, the registry's preferred product for this quantity) over the Ozone Transport Region (OTC: 11 states + DC, excluding Northern Virginia) for 2024-07-15, with full valid coverage (205/205 cells, 100% valid; no quality flag variable is published for this product). The map is rendered as chart-1. Across the region, total column ozone averaged ~293.7 DU, ranging from about 285.5 DU to 304.0 DU, with a spatial standard deviation of about 4.7 DU — a fairly uniform column-ozone field with modest regional variation on this day.

Important caveat: TEMPO_O3TOT measures total-column ozone (a stratosphere-dominated quantity in Dobson Units), which is a physically different measurement from ground-level (surface) ozone concentration in ppb that EPA AQS monitors report and that drives AQI/health assessments. I attempted to pull EPA AQS surface ozone monitor data for the same area and date to give a surface-level complement, but AQS returned no active ozone monitors for the OTC area (or within 5 degrees of it) for 2024-07-15 — an insufficient_evidence result, not a sign of clean air; it simply means no monitor data was found by that search for this area/date combination. So this exploration shows only the satellite total-column view, not ground-level ozone pollution levels in the OTC on that day.
